IMPACTO DA OBESIDADE SARCOPÊNICA SOBRE O ESTRESSE
OXIDATIVO, OS FATORES INFLAMATÓRIOS E A CAPACIDADE
FUNCIONAL EM IDOSOS

Introdução: A obesidade sarcopênica, caracterizada pela coexistência de excesso
de adiposidade e redução da massa e força muscular, tem sido associada a
comprometimentos metabólicos, inflamatórios e funcionais em idosos. No entanto, os
dados sobre sua prevalência e biomarcadores relacionado s em populações idosas
fisicamente ativas inscritas em programas de promoção da saúde ainda são
limitados.Objetivos: Analisar a associação entre obesidade sarcopênica, marcadores
inflamatórios, perfil oxidativo e capacidade funcional em idosos participante s do projeto
de extensão Universidade Aberta à Terceira Idade (UNATI). Métodologia: Este estudo
transversal incluiu 119 idosos (≥55 anos) inscritos em um Programa Universitário para
Idosos no sul do Brasil (84,9% mulheres; idade média: 68,7 ± 6,8 anos). A composição
corporal foi avaliada por bioimpedância elétrica, a força muscular por dinamometria de
preensão manual e o desempenho físico pela velocidade da marcha. A sarcopenia foi
definida de acordo com os critérios do EWGSOP2 e a obesidade sarcopênica foi
identificada utilizando diferentes combinações de parâmetros de adiposidade e massa
muscular. Foram analisados marcadores metabólicos, inflamatórios e de estresse
oxidativo. As associações foram avaliadas usando testes bivariados e correlações de
Spearman (p ≤ 0,05). Resultados: A prevalência geral de obesidade sarcopênica foi de
4,2% (n = 5), variando de acordo com os critérios diagnósticos aplicados. As mulheres
apresentaram maior prevalência de baixa massa muscular esquelética (65,3% vs.
35,3%) e força de preensão manual reduzida, enquanto os homens apresentaram maior
risco de percentual de gordura (47,1% vs. 17,8%). A circunferência da panturrilha foi a
única variável significativamente associada à obesidade (p = 0,021). Entre as mulheres,
os indicado res de adiposidade correlacionaram -se positivamente com os níveis de
triglicerídeos (IMC: r = 0,263, p < 0,001; massa gorda: r = 0,295, p < 0,001), enquanto a
velocidade da marcha associou -se inversamente à peroxidação lipídica medida por
TBARS (r = −0,295, p < 0,001), indicando menor dano oxidativo com melhor desempenho
funcional. Não foram observadas diferenças significativas entre os sexos nos
marcadores glicêmicos, lipídicos, inflamatórios ou de estresse oxidativo (p >
0,05).Conclusões: Embora a prevalência de obesidade sarcopênica tenh a sido baixa

7

nesta população idosa fisicamente ativa, observaram -se associações relevantes entre
adiposidade, perfil metabólico, estresse oxidativo e desempenho funcional. Esses
achados destacam a importância da triagem precoce da composição corporal, forç a
muscular e desequilíbrio redox, mesmo em ambientes que promovem a saúde, para
prevenir o declínio funcional subclínico durante o envelhecimento.

Palavras-chave: Obesidade Sarcopênica , Estresse Oxidativo , Inflamação, Idoso,
Capacidade Funcional.

IMPACT OF SARCOPENIC OBESITY ON OXIDATIVE STRESS,
INFLAMMATORY FACTORS, AND FUNCTIONAL CAPACITY IN OLDER
ADULTS

Introduction: Sarcopenic obesity, characterized by the coexistence of excess
adiposity and reduced muscle mass and strength, has been associated with metabolic,
inflammatory, and functional impairments in older adults. However, data on its prevalence
and related biomarkers in physically active older populations enrolled in health promotion
programs are still limited. Objectives: To analyze the association between sarcopenic
obesity, inflammatory markers, oxidative profile, and functional capacity in older a dults
participating in the extension project Universidade Aberta à Terceira Idade (UNATI).
Methodology: This cross-sectional study included 119 older adults (≥55 years) enrolled
in a University Program for Older Adults in southern Brazil (84.9% women; mean age:
68.7 ± 6.8 years). Body composition was assessed by electrical bioimpedance, muscle
strength by handgrip dynamometry, and physical performance by gait speed. Sarcopenia
was defined according to EWGSOP2 criteria, and sarcopenic obesity was identified using
different combinations of adiposity and muscle mass parameters. Metabolic,
inflammatory, and oxidative stress markers were analyzed. Associations were evaluated
using bivariate tests and Spearman correlations (p ≤ 0.05). Results: The overall
prevalence of sarcopenic obesity was 4.2% (n = 5), varying according to the applied
diagnostic criteria. Women showed a higher prevalence of low skeletal muscle mass
(65.3% vs. 35.3%) and reduced handgrip strength, while men had a higher risk of body
fat percentage (47.1% vs. 17.8%). Calf circumference was the only variable significantly
associated with obesity (p = 0.021). Among women, adiposity indicators were positively
correlated with triglyceride levels (BMI: r = 0.263, p < 0.001; fat mass: r = 0.295, p <
0.001), while gait speed was inversely associated with lipid peroxidation measured by
TBARS (r = −0.295, p < 0.001), indicating lower oxidative damage with better functional
performance. No significant differences were observed between sexes in glycemic, lipid,
inflammatory, or oxidative stress markers (p > 0.05). Conclusions: Although the
prevalence of sarcopenic obesity was low in this physically active older population,
relevant associations were observed between adiposity, metabolic profile, oxidative
stress, and functional performance. These findings highlight the importance of early

9

screening of body composition, muscle strength, and redox imbalance, even in health -
promoting environments, to prevent subclinical functional decline during aging.
Keywords: Sarcopenic Obesity, Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, Older Adult,
Functional Capacity.

Introduction

Population aging is a global phenomenon that imposes important challenges to public health and is associated
with a significant increase in the prevalence of geriatric syndromes that compromise functionality, autonomy and
quality of life, with important clinical repercussions. Among these conditions, sarcopenia and obesity stand out, both
of which are strongly related to metabolic, inflammatory, and functional changes throughout the course of aging [1].
Obesity is associated with a ch ronic low-grade inflammatory state and an increased risk of metabolic and
cardiovascular diseases and insulin resistance. Sarcopenia is characterized by the progressive loss of muscle mass,
strength and physical performance, and is related to the functional decline of the elderly [2]. The coexistence of these
conditions configures sarcopenic obesity, a complex syndrome related to a higher risk of falls, hospitalizations,
functional dependence and mortality [3].
From a pathophysiological point of view, sarco penic obesity results from the interaction between chronic
systemic inflammation, insulin resistance, hormonal changes, mitochondrial dysfunction and anabolic resistance,
promoting a cycle of visceral fat accumulation and muscle loss that accelerates functional decline, even in individuals
considered active [4]. In addition, traditional anthropometric indicators, such as body mass index, are insufficient to
identify changes in body composition, requiring more specific assessments, such as bioelectrical impe dance analysis
(BIA) and functional tests [5].
Sarcopenia, alone or in association with obesity, is related to high personal, social, and economic burdens, in
addition to a higher prevalence of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, and cognitive impairm ent. In addition, it
contributes significantly to reduced quality of life, loss of functional independence, need for long -term care, and
increased mortality among the elderly [6]. In this sense, the early identification of sarcopenia, as well as its coexistence
with obesity, even in apparently healthy and active elderly people, is a central element for the planning of preventive
and comprehensive care strategies aimed at healthy aging.
Despite the growing scientific interest, studies investigating sarcopen ic obesity in elderly participants in
programs to promote active aging are still limited. Initiatives such as the Open University for the Third Age (UNATI)
have shown a positive impact on several health outcomes; however, sarcopenic obesity may be present subclinically
even in functionally active populations, which reinforces the importance of more detailed and continuous evaluations
[7].
In this context, the present study aimed to investigate the relationship between sarcopenic obesity,
inflammatory and redox profile and functional capacity in elderly participants in UNATI, aiming to contribute to early
risk screening and the development of preventive strategies that promote healthy, functional aging with better quality
of life.

Methods

This is a cross -sectional observational study, inserted in the context of the Senior Project (Health, Aging,
Nutrition, Integration and Orientation), in which specific outcomes related to body composition, functional capacity
and health biomarkers in people aged ≥55 years or older were analyzed. The research was carried out with participants
of the Open University for the Third Age Program of the State University of Western Paraná, Francisco Beltrão
campus (UNATI-FB), respecting the ethical guidelines for r esearch with human beings and with the approval of the
Research Ethics Committee (opinion no. 7,050,783; CAAE: 82364924.8.0000.0107).
The sample was composed of individuals aged ≥55 years, regularly enrolled in UNATI -FB activities, with
sufficient mobility and communication skills to perform the proposed tests. Individuals who refused to participate,
had advanced neoplastic diseases, di d not attend the collection stages, or had sensory limitations that made the
procedures unfeasible were excluded. All participants were previously informed about the objectives of the study and
signed the Informed Consent Form. Data collection was carried out individually, by prior appointment, in
Universidade Estadual do Oeste do Paraná (UNIOESTE) environments or in health units of the participating
municipalities, by a previously trained multidisciplinary team.
Sociodemographic information was obtained u sing a structured questionnaire. Anthropometric assessment
included weight, height, body mass index, waist circumference, and calf circumference. Body composition, including
fat percentage and skeletal muscle mass, was assessed by BIA, following standardized protocols [8]. Skeletal muscle
mass was estimated by a specific equation and adjusted for height, using the Janssen equation [9]. Functional capacity
was assessed by means of gait speed in a standardized course [10,11], and handgrip strength, measured with a Saehan
hydraulic dynamometer (model SH5001), considering specific cutoff points by sex and body mass index [11]. The
level of physical activity was measured using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ), in its short
version [27].
Sarcopenia was classified according to the criteria of the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older
People (EWGSOP2), considering indicators of muscle mass, strength, and physical performance [12]. Sarcopenic

14

obesity was defined by the concomitant prese nce of sarcopenia and obesity, and different combinations of adiposity
criteria (fat percentage, body mass index, and waist circumference) and muscle indicators were explored, as described
in the literature [3].
Blood collection was performed after fastin g following validated and standardized procedures, according to
the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute [15], and the samples were processed and stored appropriately for
subsequent analysis of biochemical, inflammatory, and oxidative stress biomark ers. The glycemic and lipid profile
was determined by enzymatic colorimetric methods, according to the protocol described in the manufacturer's package
insert [16]. The markers of oxidative stress were analyzed according to the protocol adapted by Lapenna et al. [17],
and the antioxidant capacity were analyzed by standardized spectrophotometric techniques, following the method
described by Vijayalakshmi et al. [18]. The immunological analysis was performed according to the protocol
described by Engvall and Perlmann, using the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method [28].
Statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, with means and standard deviations for continuous
variables and absolute and relative frequencies for categorical variables. The normality of the data was assessed using
the Shapiro-Wilk test. Comparisons between genders were performed using the student’s t-test or the Mann-Whitney
U test, according to the distribution of the data. The associations between obesity, sarcopenia crit eria, and metabolic,
inflammatory, and oxidative profiles were analyzed using the chi-square test, with calculation of prevalence ratios and
95% confidence intervals, using Fisher's exact test when appropriate. Correlations were evaluated using Spearman's
coefficient. A significance level of 5% was adopted, and the analyses were performed using SPSS version 21.0 [19].

Discussion

The present study analyzed the association among sarcopenic obesity, i nflammatory profile and
functional capacity in the elderly at UNATI, showing significant differences in body composition between the
sexes, although functional performance was preserved in most of the sample. Men had higher muscle mass and
handgrip strength, while women had higher body fat percentage and higher prevalence of low muscle mass.
These results are in line with the literature, which describes higher adiposity and lower muscle mass and
strength in women, and higher muscle mass associated with a hi gher prevalence of central obesity in men
[6,20], differences attributed to biological and hormonal factors, and to the distinct patterns of body distribution
in aging, configuring a profile that favors greater relative adiposity in women and greater amoun t of fat-free
mass in men, although both may present cardiometabolic risk related to the accumulation of abdominal fat
[22].
Even with the maintenance of gait speed and adequate levels of physical activity, a high prevalence
of low muscle mass and reduced strength was observed, especially among women, suggesting a subclinical
risk for sarcopenia. As highlighted by Pontes [23], changes in muscle mass and strength may precede evident
functional manifestations, configuring an initial stage of vulnerabi lity not yet detected by functional tests,
which reinforces the importance of early screening to prevent progression to established sarcopenia and more
pronounced functional decline.
In the present study, glycemic, lipid, inflammatory, and oxidative stress markers did not show
significant differences between the sexes. This absence of differences should be interpreted considering the
high interindividual variability typical of aging, in addition to the small sample size among men and the smaller
number of a vailable cytokine samples, which limits statistical power [24, 25]. Still, the correlation patterns
suggest biologically plausible relationships: among women, adiposity indicators correlated with triglycerides,
and better gait performance was associated with lower levels of TBARS, suggesting that functional status may
be related to lower oxidative stress. Among men, associations between adiposity, muscle mass, and TNF -α
have been observed, although these findings should be interpreted with caution due to th e small number of
observations [26,27,28].
An important result was the low prevalence of sarcopenic obesity (4.2%), with important variation
according to the criteria adopted for adiposity and sarcopenia. This result reinforces the limitation of
comparability among studies and the impact of the ope rational definition on the estimation of prevalence,
especially in samples with good functional performance. Furthermore, calf circumference was the only variable
associated with obesity, with a lower frequency of values classified as low among obese individuals. This result
may reflect limitations of the indicator in individuals with higher total BMI, since circumference can capture
non-muscle components and not adequately discriminate muscle quality, which reinforces the need to interpret
anthropometric measurements in conjunction with the assessment of strength and body composition [12].
The findings reinforce the importance of screening strategies in active aging programs that go beyond
apparent functional assessment, incorporating detailed analyses of b ody composition, muscle strength, and
metabolic markers, in order to identify conditions such as sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity early. Among the
limitations, the cross-sectional design, the small number of men, sample losses (with potential selection bi as),
the use of bioelectrical impedance, and the low prevalence of the condition stand out, restricting the
generalization of findings and hindering stratified analyses. Longitudinal studies, with larger samples, are
needed to deepen the understanding of the relationships between sarcopenic obesity, inflammation, and decline
in strength and functionality in aging.

IMPACTO DA OBESIDADE SARCOPÊNICA SOBRE O ESTRESSE
OXIDATIVO, OS FATORES INFLAMATÓRIOS E A CAPACIDADE
FUNCIONAL EM IDOSOS

Introdução: A obesidade sarcopênica, caracterizada pela coexistência de excesso
de adiposidade e redução da massa e força muscular, tem sido associada a
comprometimentos metabólicos, inflamatórios e funcionais em idosos. No entanto, os
dados sobre sua prevalência e biomarcadores relacionado s em populações idosas
fisicamente ativas inscritas em programas de promoção da saúde ainda são
limitados.Objetivos: Analisar a associação entre obesidade sarcopênica, marcadores
inflamatórios, perfil oxidativo e capacidade funcional em idosos participante s do projeto
de extensão Universidade Aberta à Terceira Idade (UNATI). Métodologia: Este estudo
transversal incluiu 119 idosos (≥55 anos) inscritos em um Programa Universitário para
Idosos no sul do Brasil (84,9% mulheres; idade média: 68,7 ± 6,8 anos). A composição
corporal foi avaliada por bioimpedância elétrica, a força muscular por dinamometria de
preensão manual e o desempenho físico pela velocidade da marcha. A sarcopenia foi
definida de acordo com os critérios do EWGSOP2 e a obesidade sarcopênica foi
identificada utilizando diferentes combinações de parâmetros de adiposidade e massa
muscular. Foram analisados marcadores metabólicos, inflamatórios e de estresse
oxidativo. As associações foram avaliadas usando testes bivariados e correlações de
Spearman (p ≤ 0,05). Resultados: A prevalência geral de obesidade sarcopênica foi de
4,2% (n = 5), variando de acordo com os critérios diagnósticos aplicados. As mulheres
apresentaram maior prevalência de baixa massa muscular esquelética (65,3% vs.
35,3%) e força de preensão manual reduzida, enquanto os homens apresentaram maior
risco de percentual de gordura (47,1% vs. 17,8%). A circunferência da panturrilha foi a
única variável significativamente associada à obesidade (p = 0,021). Entre as mulheres,
os indicado res de adiposidade correlacionaram -se positivamente com os níveis de
triglicerídeos (IMC: r = 0,263, p < 0,001; massa gorda: r = 0,295, p < 0,001), enquanto a
velocidade da marcha associou -se inversamente à peroxidação lipídica medida por
TBARS (r = −0,295, p < 0,001), indicando menor dano oxidativo com melhor desempenho
funcional. Não foram observadas diferenças significativas entre os sexos nos
marcadores glicêmicos, lipídicos, inflamatórios ou de estresse oxidativo (p >
0,05).Conclusões: Embora a prevalência de obesidade sarcopênica tenh a sido baixa

nesta população idosa fisicamente ativa, observaram -se associações relevantes entre
adiposidade, perfil metabólico, estresse oxidativo e desempenho funcional. Esses
achados destacam a importância da triagem precoce da composição corporal, forç a
muscular e desequilíbrio redox, mesmo em ambientes que promovem a saúde, para
prevenir o declínio funcional subclínico durante o envelhecimento.

IMPACT OF SARCOPENIC OBESITY ON OXIDATIVE STRESS,
INFLAMMATORY FACTORS, AND FUNCTIONAL CAPACITY IN OLDER
ADULTS

Introduction: Sarcopenic obesity, characterized by the coexistence of excess
adiposity and reduced muscle mass and strength, has been associated with metabolic,
inflammatory, and functional impairments in older adults. However, data on its prevalence
and related biomarkers in physically active older populations enrolled in health promotion
programs are still limited. Objectives: To analyze the association between sarcopenic
obesity, inflammatory markers, oxidative profile, and functional capacity in older a dults
participating in the extension project Universidade Aberta à Terceira Idade (UNATI).
Methodology: This cross-sectional study included 119 older adults (≥55 years) enrolled
in a University Program for Older Adults in southern Brazil (84.9% women; mean age:
68.7 ± 6.8 years). Body composition was assessed by electrical bioimpedance, muscle
strength by handgrip dynamometry, and physical performance by gait speed. Sarcopenia
was defined according to EWGSOP2 criteria, and sarcopenic obesity was identified using
different combinations of adiposity and muscle mass parameters. Metabolic,
inflammatory, and oxidative stress markers were analyzed. Associations were evaluated
using bivariate tests and Spearman correlations (p ≤ 0.05). Results: The overall
prevalence of sarcopenic obesity was 4.2% (n = 5), varying according to the applied
diagnostic criteria. Women showed a higher prevalence of low skeletal muscle mass
(65.3% vs. 35.3%) and reduced handgrip strength, while men had a higher risk of body
fat percentage (47.1% vs. 17.8%). Calf circumference was the only variable significantly
associated with obesity (p = 0.021). Among women, adiposity indicators were positively
correlated with triglyceride levels (BMI: r = 0.263, p < 0.001; fat mass: r = 0.295, p <
0.001), while gait speed was inversely associated with lipid peroxidation measured by
TBARS (r = −0.295, p < 0.001), indicating lower oxidative damage with better functional
performance. No significant differences were observed between sexes in glycemic, lipid,
inflammatory, or oxidative stress markers (p > 0.05). Conclusions: Although the
prevalence of sarcopenic obesity was low in this physically active older population,
relevant associations were observed between adiposity, metabolic profile, oxidative
stress, and functional performance. These findings highlight the importance of early

9

screening of body composition, muscle strength, and redox imbalance, even in health -
promoting environments, to prevent subclinical functional decline during aging.
Keywords: Sarcopenic Obesity, Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, Older Adult,
Functional Capacity.

IMPACT OF SARCOPENIC OBESITY ON OXIDATIVE STRESS, INFLAMMATORY FACTORS, AND
FUNCTIONAL CAPACITY IN OLDER ADULTS

Background: Sarcopenic obesity, characterized by the coexistence of excess adiposity and reduced muscle mass and
strength, has been associated with metabolic, inflammatory, and functional impairments in older adults. However,
data on its prevalence and related biomarkers in physically active older populations enrolled in health promotion
programs remain limited. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 119 older adults (≥55 years) enrolled in a
University Program for Older Adults in southern Brazil (84.9% women; mean age: 68.7 ± 6.8 years). Body
composition was assessed using bioelectrical impedance analysis, muscle s trength by handgrip dynamometry, and
physical performance by gait speed. Sarcopenia was defined according to EWGSOP2 criteria, and sarcopenic obesity
was identified using different combinations of adiposity and muscle mass parameters. Metabolic, inflammato ry, and
oxidative stress markers were analyzed. Associations were evaluated using bivariate tests and Spearman correlations
(p ≤ 0.05). Results: The overall prevalence of sarcopenic obesity was 4.2% (n = 5), varying according to the diagnostic
criteria applied. Women showed a higher prevalence of low skeletal muscle mass (65.3% vs. 35.3%) and reduced
handgrip strength, while men had a higher risk of elevated body fat percentage (47.1% vs. 17.8%). Calf circumference
was the only variable significantly associ ated with obesity (p = 0.021). Among women, adiposity indicators were
positively correlated with triglyceride levels (BMI: r = 0.263, p < 0.001; fat mass: r = 0.295, p < 0.001), whereas gait
speed was inversely associated with lipid peroxidation measured by TBARS (r = −0.295, p < 0.001), indicating lower
oxidative damage with better functional performance. No significant sex differences were observed in glycemic, lipid,
inflammatory, or oxidative stress markers (p > 0.05). Conclusions: Although the prevalen ce of sarcopenic obesity
was low in this physically active older population, relevant associations were observed between adiposity, metabolic
profile, oxidative stress, and functional performance. These findings highlight the importance of early screening of
body composition, muscle strength, and redox imbalance, even in health -promoting settings, to prevent subclinical
functional decline during aging.
Keywords: Sarcopenic Obesity; Oxidative Stress; Inflammation; Older Adults; Functional Capacity.

Introduction

Population aging is a global phenomenon that imposes important challenges to public health and is associated
with a significant increase in the prevalence of geriatric syndromes that compromise functionality, autonomy and
quality of life, with important clinical repercussions. Among these conditions, sarcopenia and obesity stand out, both
of which are strongly related to metabolic, inflammatory, and functional changes throughout the course of aging [1].
Obesity is associated with a ch ronic low-grade inflammatory state and an increased risk of metabolic and
cardiovascular diseases and insulin resistance. Sarcopenia is characterized by the progressive loss of muscle mass,
strength and physical performance, and is related to the functional decline of the elderly [2]. The coexistence of these
conditions configures sarcopenic obesity, a complex syndrome related to a higher risk of falls, hospitalizations,
functional dependence and mortality [3].
From a pathophysiological point of view, sarco penic obesity results from the interaction between chronic
systemic inflammation, insulin resistance, hormonal changes, mitochondrial dysfunction and anabolic resistance,
promoting a cycle of visceral fat accumulation and muscle loss that accelerates functional decline, even in individuals
considered active [4]. In addition, traditional anthropometric indicators, such as body mass index, are insufficient to
identify changes in body composition, requiring more specific assessments, such as bioelectrical impe dance analysis
(BIA) and functional tests [5].
Sarcopenia, alone or in association with obesity, is related to high personal, social, and economic burdens, in
addition to a higher prevalence of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, and cognitive impairm ent. In addition, it
contributes significantly to reduced quality of life, loss of functional independence, need for long -term care, and
increased mortality among the elderly [6]. In this sense, the early identification of sarcopenia, as well as its coexistence
with obesity, even in apparently healthy and active elderly people, is a central element for the planning of preventive
and comprehensive care strategies aimed at healthy aging.
Despite the growing scientific interest, studies investigating sarcopen ic obesity in elderly participants in
programs to promote active aging are still limited. Initiatives such as the Open University for the Third Age (UNATI)
have shown a positive impact on several health outcomes; however, sarcopenic obesity may be present subclinically
even in functionally active populations, which reinforces the importance of more detailed and continuous evaluations
[7].
In this context, the present study aimed to investigate the relationship between sarcopenic obesity,
inflammatory and redox profile and functional capacity in elderly participants in UNATI, aiming to contribute to early
risk screening and the development of preventive strategies that promote healthy, functional aging with better quality
of life.

Methods

This is a cross -sectional observational study, inserted in the context of the Senior Project (Health, Aging,
Nutrition, Integration and Orientation), in which specific outcomes related to body composition, functional capacity
and health biomarkers in people aged ≥55 years or older were analyzed. The research was carried out with participants
of the Open University for the Third Age Program of the State University of Western Paraná, Francisco Beltrão
campus (UNATI-FB), respecting the ethical guidelines for r esearch with human beings and with the approval of the
Research Ethics Committee (opinion no. 7,050,783; CAAE: 82364924.8.0000.0107).
The sample was composed of individuals aged ≥55 years, regularly enrolled in UNATI -FB activities, with
sufficient mobility and communication skills to perform the proposed tests. Individuals who refused to participate,
had advanced neoplastic diseases, di d not attend the collection stages, or had sensory limitations that made the
procedures unfeasible were excluded. All participants were previously informed about the objectives of the study and
signed the Informed Consent Form. Data collection was carried out individually, by prior appointment, in
Universidade Estadual do Oeste do Paraná (UNIOESTE) environments or in health units of the participating
municipalities, by a previously trained multidisciplinary team.
Sociodemographic information was obtained u sing a structured questionnaire. Anthropometric assessment
included weight, height, body mass index, waist circumference, and calf circumference. Body composition, including
fat percentage and skeletal muscle mass, was assessed by BIA, following standardized protocols [8]. Skeletal muscle
mass was estimated by a specific equation and adjusted for height, using the Janssen equation [9]. Functional capacity
was assessed by means of gait speed in a standardized course [10,11], and handgrip strength, measured with a Saehan
hydraulic dynamometer (model SH5001), considering specific cutoff points by sex and body mass index [11]. The
level of physical activity was measured using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ), in its short
version [27].
Sarcopenia was classified according to the criteria of the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older
People (EWGSOP2), considering indicators of muscle mass, strength, and physical performance [12]. Sarcopenic

obesity was defined by the concomitant prese nce of sarcopenia and obesity, and different combinations of adiposity
criteria (fat percentage, body mass index, and waist circumference) and muscle indicators were explored, as described
in the literature [3].
Blood collection was performed after fastin g following validated and standardized procedures, according to
the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute [15], and the samples were processed and stored appropriately for
subsequent analysis of biochemical, inflammatory, and oxidative stress biomark ers. The glycemic and lipid profile
was determined by enzymatic colorimetric methods, according to the protocol described in the manufacturer's package
insert [16]. The markers of oxidative stress were analyzed according to the protocol adapted by Lapenna et al. [17],
and the antioxidant capacity were analyzed by standardized spectrophotometric techniques, following the method
described by Vijayalakshmi et al. [18]. The immunological analysis was performed according to the protocol
described by Engvall and Perlmann, using the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method [28].
Statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, with means and standard deviations for continuous
variables and absolute and relative frequencies for categorical variables. The normality of the data was assessed using
the Shapiro-Wilk test. Comparisons between genders were performed using the student’s t-test or the Mann-Whitney
U test, according to the distribution of the data. The associations between obesity, sarcopenia crit eria, and metabolic,
inflammatory, and oxidative profiles were analyzed using the chi-square test, with calculation of prevalence ratios and
95% confidence intervals, using Fisher's exact test when appropriate. Correlations were evaluated using Spearman's
coefficient. A significance level of 5% was adopted, and the analyses were performed using SPSS version 21.0 [19].

Discussion

The present study analyzed the association among sarcopenic obesity, i nflammatory profile and
functional capacity in the elderly at UNATI, showing significant differences in body composition between the
sexes, although functional performance was preserved in most of the sample. Men had higher muscle mass and
handgrip strength, while women had higher body fat percentage and higher prevalence of low muscle mass.
These results are in line with the literature, which describes higher adiposity and lower muscle mass and
strength in women, and higher muscle mass associated with a hi gher prevalence of central obesity in men
[6,20], differences attributed to biological and hormonal factors, and to the distinct patterns of body distribution
in aging, configuring a profile that favors greater relative adiposity in women and greater amoun t of fat-free
mass in men, although both may present cardiometabolic risk related to the accumulation of abdominal fat
[22].
Even with the maintenance of gait speed and adequate levels of physical activity, a high prevalence
of low muscle mass and reduced strength was observed, especially among women, suggesting a subclinical
risk for sarcopenia. As highlighted by Pontes [23], changes in muscle mass and strength may precede evident
functional manifestations, configuring an initial stage of vulnerabi lity not yet detected by functional tests,
which reinforces the importance of early screening to prevent progression to established sarcopenia and more
pronounced functional decline.
In the present study, glycemic, lipid, inflammatory, and oxidative stress markers did not show
significant differences between the sexes. This absence of differences should be interpreted considering the
high interindividual variability typical of aging, in addition to the small sample size among men and the smaller
number of a vailable cytokine samples, which limits statistical power [24, 25]. Still, the correlation patterns
suggest biologically plausible relationships: among women, adiposity indicators correlated with triglycerides,
and better gait performance was associated with lower levels of TBARS, suggesting that functional status may
be related to lower oxidative stress. Among men, associations between adiposity, muscle mass, and TNF -α
have been observed, although these findings should be interpreted with caution due to th e small number of
observations [26,27,28].
An important result was the low prevalence of sarcopenic obesity (4.2%), with important variation
according to the criteria adopted for adiposity and sarcopenia. This result reinforces the limitation of
comparability among studies and the impact of the ope rational definition on the estimation of prevalence,
especially in samples with good functional performance. Furthermore, calf circumference was the only variable
associated with obesity, with a lower frequency of values classified as low among obese individuals. This result
may reflect limitations of the indicator in individuals with higher total BMI, since circumference can capture
non-muscle components and not adequately discriminate muscle quality, which reinforces the need to interpret
anthropometric measurements in conjunction with the assessment of strength and body composition [12].
The findings reinforce the importance of screening strategies in active aging programs that go beyond
apparent functional assessment, incorporating detailed analyses of b ody composition, muscle strength, and
metabolic markers, in order to identify conditions such as sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity early. Among the
limitations, the cross-sectional design, the small number of men, sample losses (with potential selection bi as),
the use of bioelectrical impedance, and the low prevalence of the condition stand out, restricting the
generalization of findings and hindering stratified analyses. Longitudinal studies, with larger samples, are
needed to deepen the understanding of the relationships between sarcopenic obesity, inflammation, and decline
in strength and functionality in aging.
